sources.title: J. K. Patnaik, Excavations at Lalitagiri (1985–1991), Memoirs of the Archaeological Survey of India 112 (2016)
sources.locator: Chapter I, A. The Site and its Environs, opening page, PDF p.25; title PDF p.3, edition/copyright PDF p.4
sources.access: Original 415-page PDF downloaded; only title/edition/foreword and chapter opening inspected; title and chapter page rendered and visually read. Not a review of entire book.
claims: Lalitagiri village lies among Nandapahara, Parabhadi and Olasuni hills.
These hills are isolated Assia-range spurs, described as an offshoot of the Eastern Ghats.
Low-lying fertile alluvial plains surround these hills, associated with Gobari drainage.
Olasuni is remembered for the cenotaph of nineteenth-century saint Arakshita Das.
limits: Approach distances and transport paragraph concern Lalitagiri, not Olasuni: do not transfer.
Rock composition, caves, quarrying and microwave tower later on page concern Parabhadi: do not transfer.
Cenotaph attribution does not date present temple construction or prove saints’ birth/death dates.

sources.title: Significance
sources.access: Original web-page body retrieved through web tool and read; no direct HTML archive.
claims: Committee identifies Gumpha Ekadasi/Olasuni Yatra as commemorating Arakshita Das.
It describes shared prasada irrespective of caste and frames the festival around human fellowship.
It lists podapitha, khechudi and dahipakhal among offerings.
limits: Attribute religious practice and ideals to the committee; no guarantee that a visitor can obtain food on a given day.
Omit ancient Buddhist chronology in boilerplate and fixed Gregorian festival dates/duration.
About/How To Reach pages from same committee are one source family, not corroboration.

sources.family: Ashis Senapati / Times of India original reporting
sources.title: Olasuni mela serves as platform for crafts
sources.author: Ashis Senapati
sources.access: Original publisher page opened and full article body read.
claims: Report places the 2025 mela at Olasuni hillock in Jajpur.
Report describes samadhi worship and sales of stone grinders, household goods and carved figures.
Reporting includes nearby stone artisans and brass craftspersons.
limits: Date all fair descriptions to 2025; no upcoming dates, stock, prices or vendor-presence promises.
Do not adopt precise chronology, royal genealogy, manuscript chapter count or festival age from this report without further evidence.
Names/testimony in source remain reported testimony, not our interviews.
